## Radio Theory

production of radio wave: oscillating electrical current and an aerial (antenna)   
electrons moving back and forth in aerial produce changing electrical field   
electrical field moves "away" from aerial at speed of light   
"receiving" aerial induces "identical" current   
amplifiers and filters compensate for power loss of signal at receiving end

transmitter --> transmitter aerial ........ receiving aerial --> receiver --> amplifier -> headset

waves are referred to in terms of frequence or wavelength   
speed of light ~ constant (in vacuum) 300.000.000 $\frac{m}{s}$ = $3 * 10^8 \frac{m}{s}$.
= $162.000 \frac{NM}{s}$

cycles per second = frequency   
doubline frequency will halve the wavelenght, i.e. 2 cycles per second

1000Hz = 1 kHz, 1.000.000Hz = 1MHz, 1.000.000.000Hz = 1GHz

wavelength $\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$

note: for calculations use right units:    
* wavelength $\lambda$: metres
* frequency $f$:        Hz = $\frac{m}{s}$

example: radio signal of 3kHz - find wavelength: $\lambda = \frac{c}{f} =\frac{3 * 10^8}{3 * 10^3} = 10^5m = 100km$

Radio signal has wavelength of 3.5cm. What is the frequency?
$\lambda = 3.5 cm = 3.5 * 10^{-2}m$
$f = \frac{c}{\lambda} = \frac{3 * 10^8 m/s}{3.5 * 10^{-2}m} = \frac{3}{3.5}*10^{10}\frac{1}{s}$
$f = 0.857 * 10 * 10^9 Hz =8.57 GHz$

### Frequency Spectrum

radio spectrum is part of electromagnetic spectrum and covers frequencies from 3kHz to 300GHz.   
spectrum browken down into 8 bands ranging from Very Low Frequencies VLF to Extremetly High Frequencies EHF.

military uses upper VHF and UHF bands for communications.   
civil agencies use the VHF badn from 118MHz to 137 MHz.

Channel spacing now -- in Europe -- 8.33kHz (used to be 25 kHz) ~ increase in number of channels.   
reception (power) usually good when in range

range affected by    
* power of transmitter
* height of transmitter and receiver
* obstracutions between transmitter and receiver.

civil communication is also conducted on HF frequencies between 2.8MHz and 22.0MHz.
These frequencies give long range, over the horizon capbailty

### Maximum Theroretical Range

max theoretical range NM = $1.23 * \sqrt{height\ transmitter(ft_{AMSL})} + 1.23 * \sqrt{height\ receiver(ft_{AMSL})}$   
range in NM ~ both heights in feet AMSL

range represents line of sight plus an element of ducting.    
Ducting is a phenonmenon in which - under certain atmospheric condistion - a radio wave may be 'ducted' or 'guided' along a narrow horizontal layer following the Earth's curvature.    
This invariably results in an increase in the wave's transmission range.

Example: maximum distance for a VHF contact over flat terrain at FL100?   
no info on receiver ~ h2 := 0    
FL100 ~ 10.000ft AMSL   
==> $1.23 * \sqrt{10^4} = 1.23 * 10^2 = 123NM$

What is the approximate VHF range for an ac at FL80 and an aeronautical station at 325ft MSL?

range NM = $1.23 * \sqrt{8000} + 1.23 * \sqrt{325}$    
= $1.23 * \sqrt{9*9*10^3} + 1.23 * 18 = 1.23 * 9 * 10 + 22.14 = 110,7 + 22,14 = 132NM$

ac range is 115NM, FE 169ft. Min FL to receive VHF signal?

$R = 1.23 \sqrt{H1} + 1.23 \sqrt{H2}$    
$\frac{R - 1.23 \sqrt{H1}}{1.23} = \sqrt{H2$    
$H2 = (\frac{R - 1.23 \sqrt{H1}}{1.23})^2$
$H2 = (115 - 1.23 * 13)^2/(1.23)^2$   
$H2 = (99 / 1.23)^2 = 6460ft = FL65$

### Power

power output of a transmitter affects its range.   
200W outputs --> 200NM, 50NM --> short range transmissions.

Doubling of range requires 4 * power.

==> if ac twice as far from transmitter, received power  1/4 of original strength

### Attenuation

Attenuation is the loss of signal strength of a wave.   
In vaccum there is no attenuation as the radio wave has nothing to give up its energy to.   
Waves passing through atmosphere, dust and water droplets absorb some of the energy = atmosphereic attenuation.

attentuation increases with increasing frequency   
attentuation significant > 1 GHz

waves passing over Earth's surface lose energy and slow down.   
surface attentuation is greatest and speed is lowest over the ice cap, then desert areas, then over other land; least attentuation over sea

surface attentuation increases as frequency increases similar to atmosphereic attentuation.   
rock and water affect both.

waves passing through layers of electrically charged atoms at the edge  of space, i.e., ionosphere, are likewise attenuated.   
ionospheric attenuation increases with lower (decreasing) frequencies (i.e., opposite effect)

attenuation is the loss of power in waves.   
atmospheric and surface attenuation is greatest with high frequencies.   
ionospheric attenuation is greatest at low frequencies.

### Adding Information

frequency of a wave on its own is not audible - cannot be heard as a single tone.
any information to be transmitted myst be "laid on top" of the carriert wave before transmission and decoded by the receiver.   
This process is known as modulation and demodulation.

#### Amplitude Modulation

simplest form of modulation := vary the strength or the amplitude of the carrier wave to transmit inforamtion.   
VHF, UHF, and HF comms use amplitude modulation AM.

modulation is the addition of information to a carrier wave.

#### Frequency Modulation

alternative form of modulation ~ vary the frequency. == frequency modulation FM

although FM receiver wil pick up the same interference and static with the signal as an AM receiveer, it has the capability to "clip" the signal to remove any extraneous variations in amplitude.   
The variation in frequency which can carry the intelligence are unaffected.   
Thus, an FM audio signal will produce a high fidelity reporuductionof the original without interference from static.

FM more complex - but reduces static.

#### Pulse Modulation

information such as Morse signals can be transmitted by interrupting the carrier wave to send a series of dots and dashes.   
more complex systems can use pulse modulation to send digitised information in a binaray code.

PM sends digital data or morse code.


### Summary

radio waves are the name given to a specific band of frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.   
radio waves travel at the speed of light, approx 300.000.000m/s = 3*1-^8 m/s.

radio waves are generated by passing an oscillating electircal current through an aerial.   
each oscillation produces one wave

relationship; wavelength $\lambda$ = $\frac{c}{f}$

information is carried by altering the radio wave's freququency or its amplitude, i.e., the wave is "modulated".

radio frequency spectrum is divided into 8 bands ranging from very low to extremely high frequency.   
Factors affecting the range of VHF and UHF signals are:    
* power of the transmitter
* height of the transmitter and the receiver
* obstructions between transmitter and receiver

The maximum theoretical range of a VHF or UHF signal is given by: max range (NM) = $1.23 \sqrt{H1(ft\ AMSL)} + 1.23 \sqrt{H2(ft\ AMSL)}$

## Categories of Messages

"aeronautical mobile service" := (ICAO) air to air or ground to air communications

aeronautical station := ground station    
"aeronautical fixed service" := communication between ground stations

### AFTN

aeronautical fixed telecommunication network (AFTN) ~ network of text type messaging between ground (fixed) stations

AFTN ~ world wide system of aeronautical fixed circuuits  -> exchange of messages and/or digitla data between aeronautical fixed stations having the same or compatible communication characteristics

telecommunication := any transmission, emission, or reception of sign, signals, writing, images, and sounds or intelligence of any nature by wire, radio, optical or other electromagnetic systems.

### Message Categories

radio messages in the aeronautical mobise serveice fall into one of 6 different categories.    
priority dependent on category

* distress calls, distress messages, and distress traffic "MAYDAY"
* urgency messages, incld. messages preceded by medicatl transport signal "PAN PAN" or "PAN PAN MEDICAL"
* communication related to direction finding
* flight safety messages
* meteorological messages
* flight regularity messages

### Distress Messages

distress := ac or pax are threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and require immediate assistance

ac: 
* "MAYDAY" preferrably 3 times   
* MAYDAY call on frequency in use, 121.5MHz or other distress frequencies when unable to contact aeronautical station on freq in use   
* under radar contact maintain allocated SSR code unless instructed to change to 7700

MAYDAY message to consist of as many as possible    
* name of station being addresses (if time and circumstances permit)
* identification of aircraft
* nature of distress
* intention of person in command
* present position
* level or altitude
* aircraft heading

response ~ first station acknowledging distress message   
* immediately acknowledge distress message
* take control of communications or clearly transfer that responsibility, advising the aircraft if a transfer is made;
* take immediate action to ensure that all necessary information is made available, as soon as possible to 
  + ATS unit concerned;
  + aircraft operating agency concerned, or its representative, in accordance with teh pre-etablished arrangements; and
* warn other stations, as appropriate, to prevent the transfer of traffic to the frequency of the distress communication

Imposition of silence

The station in distress, or the station in conteol of distress traffic, may impose silence, either on all stations of the mobile service in the area or on any station that interferes with the distress traffic.    
It may address these instructions: "TO ALL STATIONS", or to one station only, according to circumstances by ".... STOP TRANSMITTING" together with the distress signal "MAYDAY".

action by all "other" stations

distress comms have priority over all other communications   
stations aware of a distress situation/communication must not transmit on the frequency concerned, unless    
* distress is cancelled or distress traffic is terminated
* all distress traffic has been transferred to other frequencies known as discrete frequencies DEF
* station contolling communications gives permission
* it is obliged to render assistance

termination of distress communication and of silence

ac no longer in distress, mut transmit message cancelling the distress condition

distress communication and silence conditions are terminated by transmitting a message including the words DISTRESS TRAFFIC ENDED on frequencies being used for distress traffic


frequencies can be truncated 119.100 := ONE ONE NINEr DECIMAL ONE

only the station controlling the communication can terminate distress communication/silence

### Urgency Messages

urgency := condition concerning the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of some person on board or within sight, but which does not require immediate assistance.

PAN message also used for medical transports.    
medical transports defined in 1949 Geneva Conventions and Addional Protocols := any means of transportation by land, water, or air; whether military or civilian, permanent or temporary, assigned exclusively to medical transportation and under the control of a competent authority of a party to the conflict.

ac reporting urgency condition:

in general, urgency message preceded by the phrase PAN PAN, preferable spoke 3 times

PAN prefix also used by medical transports.

urgency message to be sent by ac reporting urgency condition on the air-ground frequency in use comprising    

* name of station addressed
* identification of aircraft
* nature of urgency
* intention of the person in command
* preswent position, level / altitude, and heading
* any other useful information

action to be taken in reply

first station receiving urgency message shall

* immediately acknowledge the urgency message
* if necessary, exercise control of communications;
* take immediate action to ensure that all necessary infromation is made available, as soon as possible to:
  + ATS unit concerned; and
  + the aircraft operating agency concerned, or its representative, in accordance with the pre-established arrangements
  
Urgency communication have priority over all other commununications, ecept distress, and all stations should teake care not to interfere with the transmission of urgency traffic

action by aircraft used for medical transports

PAN PAN * 3 MEDICAL

* callsign or other recognised means of identification of the medical transports
* position of the medical transports
* number and type of medical transports
* intended route
* estimated time en route and of departure and arrival, as appropriate
* any other information such as flight altitude, reaio frequeniceis guarded, languatges used, and secondary surveillance radar modes and codes.


### Direction Finding DF

some VHF ground stations are equipped with automatic direction finding VHF DF    
military stations may provide VHF DF or UHF DF

bearing information can be provided on request expressed as either a magnetic or true direction either to or from the station.   
Bearings from 2 DF stations can provide a fix.   

* QTE ~ true bearing from the station  (True Emanation)
* QUJ ~ true bearing to the station
* QDR ~ magnetic bearing from the station (Direction on Radial)
* QDM ~ magnetic bearing to station (Direction to Mama)

stations providing VHF DF are listed in AIP.   
Some VDF are not available for enroute navigation pruposes except in emergency.   
VDF bearing will only be given when conditions are satisfactory and radio bearings fall within calibrated limits of the station. 
If a readio bearing cannot be given the pilot will be told why.

note: bearing accurace of -/+5deg most common, i.e., class not given

VDF fxing --> VDF from a single station do not provide a position fix. To objtain a fix several CDF stations must be operating on the same frequency at the same time.   
This only occurs on the VHF Emergency Frequency 121.5 MHz.

Fixing accuracy    
* class A ~ accurate within  5NM
* class B ~ accurate within 20NM
* class C ~ accurate within 50NM
* class D ~ accurate less than C (> 50NM)


### Flight Safety Messages

flight safety messages include

* movement and control messages
* messages originated by an aircraft operationg agency or be an aircraft, of immediatee concernt to an aircraft in flight
* meteorological advice of immediate concern to an ac in flight or about to depart (individually communicated or for broadcast)
* other messages concerning aircraft in flight or about to depart

"most" communication between ATC and ac fall into this category.


### Meteorological Messages

meteorological messages are messages to or from aircraft which contain meteorological information other than that listed as flight safety message.

### Flight Regularity Messages

flight regularity messages comprise:

* messages regardin the operation or maintenance of facilities essential for the regularity of aircraft operation;
* messages concerning the servicing of aircraft
* instructions to aircraft operating agency representatives concerning change in requirements fror passengers and crew caused by unavoidable deviations from normal operating schedules. Individual requirements of passengers or crew shall not be admissible in this type of message.
* messages concerning non-routine landings to be made by the aircraft;
* messages concerning aircraft parts and materials urgently requireed;
* messages concerning changes in aircraft operating schedules.

### Summary

AFTN provides communication between ground stations using the AFTN network

6 categories of messages   
* distress ("MAYDAY")
* urgency ("PAN PAN") or PAN MEDICAL transport
* direction finding DF
* flight safety
* meteorological
* flight regularity

distress := ac or pax are threatened by serious and immediate danger and require immediate assistance    
urgency := condition concerning the safety of an ac or its pax which does not require immediate assistance (!= distress)

VHF ground stations may provide automatic direction finding
  + class A ~ accurate to -/+2deg
  + class B ~ most common, accurate to -/+5deg

VDF position fix from 2 or more stations are also categories
  + class A ~ accurate within 5NM (9.3km)
  + class B ~ accurate within 20NM (37km)




## Radio Techniques

standardised R/T --> reduce risk of misunderstanding/interpretation   
ICAO recommends "standard phraseology" or plain language.

"mach's Maul auf & hör bald auf!", adequate speed, no fillers, PTT   
no response ~ wait about 10secs   
do not use OVER or OUT (only to clarify, if needed)

stuck mic ~ transmit button is held of stuck ~ frequency unusable by others

### Transmission of Time

times are given in UTC   
usually only "minutes" (as hour known) - use hour if there is any possibility of confustion

### Transmission of Letters

exception of telephony designator and the type of aircraft, each letter in the aircraft callsign should be spoken separately using the phonetic spelling.

### Transmission of Numbers

3500  THREE THOUSAND FIVE HUNDRED
25000 TWO FIVE THOUSAND

use DECIMAL

### Standard Words and Phrases

ACKNOWLEDGE let me know that you have received and understood this message
AFFIRM      yes
APPROVED    permission for proposed action granted
BREAK       indicate separtion between portion of the messge
BREAK BREAK indicate separation between messages transmmitted to different aircraftin a very busy environment
CANCEL      annul previously transmitted clearance
CHECK       examin a system or procedure; no answer is normally expected
CLEARD      authorised to proceed under the conditions specified
CONFIRM     I request clarification of ...
CONTACT     establis radio contact with ...
CORRECT     true or accurate
CORRECTION  an error has been made in this transmission (or message indicated) ... the correrct version is ...
DISREGARD   ignore
HOW DO YOU READ
I SAY AGAIN I repeat for clarity or emphasis
MAINTAIN    continue in accordance with the condition(s) specified or in its literal sense (e.g. MAINTAIN VFR)
MONITOR     listen out on ... (frequency)
NEGATIVE    no or permission not granted, this is not correct
OUT         this exchange of transmission is ended, no response expected
OVER        my transmission ended, I expect a response from you
READ BACK   repeat all, or the specified part of this message back to me exactly as received
RECLEARED   a change has been made to your last clearance and the new clearance supersedes your previous clearance or part thereof
REPORT      pass me the following information
REQUEST     I wish to know ... I wish to obtain ...
ROGER       I have received all of your last transmission
SAY AGAIN   repeat all, or the following part of your last transmission
SPEAK SLOWER  reduce your rate of speech
STAND BY    wait and I will call you
UNABLE      I cannot comply with your ... (request, instruction, ...), normally followed by reason
WILCO       I understand your message and will comply
WORDS TWICE - as a request: communication is difficult, please send every word/group twice
            - as information: as comms are difficult, each word/group will be sent twice

### Callsigns

aeronautical stations are identified by the name of the location followed by a suffic.   
suffix indicates type of unit or service

if satisfactory communication has been established and provided that it will not be confusin, the name of the location or callsign suffix may be omitted: LANGEN APPROACH --> LANGEN or APPROACH

* area control center ACC   CONTROL
* radar (in general)        RADAR
* approach control          APPROACH
* approach control radar arrivals   ARRIVAL
* approach control radar departures DEPARTURE
* aerodrome control         TOWER
* surface movement control  GROUND
* clearance delivery        DELIVERY
* precision approach radar  PRECISION
* direction finding station HOMER
* flight information service  INFORMATION
* appron control/management APRON
* company dispatch          DISPATCH
* aeronautical station      RADIO

### Aircraft Callsign

commercial aircraft may use either their aircraft registration or -- more commonly -- an R/T designator approved by ICAO plus the flight number.   
For example, British Airways designator is "SPEEDBIRD" (BAW), Aer Lingus "SHAMROCK"

change of callsign --> likelihood that confusion may occur because of similr callsigns, an aircraft may unusually, be instructed by an air traffic control unit to temporarily change the type of its callsign

ATC: CHANGE YOUR CALLSIGN TO .... [UNTIL FURTHER ADVISED]

REVERT TO FLIGHT PLAN CALLSIGN .... [AT significant point]

Aircraft in the HEAVY WTC, MTOW > 136.000kg, include HEAVY immediately after the aircraft callsign in the initial call to the aerodrome control tower and the approach control unit   
SUPER in case of A380.


### Summary

times are given in UTC - usually only minutes (unless risk of confusion)

aeronautical stations are identified by the name of the location followed by a suffix. suffix indicates the type of unit or service provided

general aviation aircraft and private ac use the aircraft registration as the callsign.   
commercial aviaition normally use R/T designator approved by ICAO followed by the flight number

aircraft is not allowed to change its type of callsign or alter its callsign during flight other than adopting ATC's abbreviation.   
If necessary, ATC may instruct an ac to change its callsign.

Initial call to an aerodrome control tower or approach control unit, an ac in HEAVY WTC must include HEAVY (or SUPER) immediately after the callsign.
